# SpeedProfiling Project (Baylor Football Velocity Profiling)

SpeedProfiling is a Baylor football velocity-profiling project that pulls full-game 10 Hz Catapult GPS data, aligns it with college football play-by-play (via CFBD / cfbfastR), and produces per-athlete speed/velocity profiles adapted from a workshop method authored by "Alex." The project is developed as a private R repository (`github.com/erash11/SpeedProfiling`, 176-package renv lockfile) executed against a 7-ticket implementation plan tracked in the KeystoneOS `.scratch/speedprofiling/issues/` directory, using the mattpocock `implement` and `code-review` skills. On 2026-07-18, tickets 01, 02, 04, and 07 were advanced; on 2026-07-20, ticket 05 (GPS↔play-by-play merge, on-field separation, workload tables) was closed and shipped on PR #3.

## Key Points

- **Ticket-driven, per-session workflow:** the project is decomposed into 7 tickets; each ticket is implemented in a fresh session via `/mattpocock-skills:implement <ticket path>`. The `Status:` line in each ticket file is the claim mechanism that prevents parallel-session collisions. Eric prefers fresh parallel sessions per ticket over driving all tickets from one session.
- **catapultR credentials-object API change:** the installed catapultR uses a new credentials-object API — `ofCloudCreateToken(sToken=…, sRegion='America')`; the old `token=` argument no longer exists. `R/01_get_data.R` was rewritten for this API in ticket 04.
- **Full 10 Hz pull verified (ticket 04):** the pull retrieved 8,932,931 rows at true 10 Hz (0.1 s spacing, max velocity 20.3 mph) for all 61/61 athletes (79 MB, gitignored) plus 188 play-by-play plays; 69/69 testthat tests pass. A feasibility probe gate hard-stops before the bulk pull unless genuine 10 Hz rows with all required columns return.
- **Ticket 05 — GPS↔play-by-play alignment (2026-07-20):** merged 10 Hz GPS with play-by-play using the kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor, separated on-field from sideline athletes via a two-part rule (sideline boundary + metabolic-power gate), and produced per-play workload tables. Closed on PR #3. See [[concepts/speedprofiling-gps-playbyplay-alignment]].
- **Game selection is config, not code:** game selection moved from hardcoded `GAME_*` variables to a `GAMES` table in `R/config.R` (activity ID + cfbd args per row). Adding a game is a one-row config edit; an empty `GAMES` renders the activity list to pick from. Per-game `.rds` caching pays the slow pull once.
- **Stacked PRs merge in order #1 → #2 → #3;** ticket 04's PR #2 is stacked on ticket 03's PR #1.

## Details

The project adopts a set of workshop R scripts (from an author "Alex") as reference material and re-implements them ticket by ticket against Baylor's live data sources. Ticket 01 established the repo, adopted the Drive scripts/docs, and set FERPA rules in AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md adapter, gitignore protection, and a private repo. A standards review of the adopted scripts found four real defects — notably a timestamp-conversion bug in `01_get_data.R` and play-end windows in `02_combine_data.R` that erroneously absorb halftime gaps — which were logged to the tracker and mapped to downstream tickets 03–06 rather than patched twice in reference code. Ticket 02 decoded the Catapult JWT scopes (`connect, catapultr, sensor-read-only`, expiry 2126), confirming the sensor scope needed for the 10 Hz feasibility probe, and migrated tokens from an untracked `AccessTokens.txt` (hardened out via `.gitignore` patterns `AccessTokens.txt` and `*token*.txt`) into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\.Renviron` (`CATAPULT_TOKEN`, `CFBD_API_KEY`).

Ticket 04 delivered the core game-data pull (8.9M rows at true 10 Hz for 61 athletes), verified end-to-end (69/69 tests, both `.rds` caches hit on re-run). The BYU game (BYU – G5 – 09.28.24) was auto-selected because ticket 02 had already verified its play-by-play and Eric was unavailable to pick interactively; swapping games is a one-row `GAMES` config edit. Ticket 04 anticipated two forward-looking findings for ticket 05: Catapult X/Y coordinates return in venue coordinates requiring a transform, and the cfbfastR `wallclock` column might simplify GPS↔play timestamp alignment. Ticket 05 (2026-07-20) resolved both — the venue-coordinate issue via PCA field-frame recovery and the timestamp alignment via the kickoff surge signature rather than `wallclock`. A recurring environment note: background R tasks can report a false "exit code 1" even when the script log shows a clean end-to-end run, so the log must be checked before assuming failure (see [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). Ticket 03 (analysis core + tests) and ticket 07 (KeystoneOS/SecondBrain integration) were also run as parallel fresh sessions, and ticket 06 (velocity profiles — sprint detection, NLS fits, bootstrap CIs, position-group comparisons) remains downstream.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Athlete Monitoring / Return-to-Play Conference Presentation Design

On 2026-06-17, a conference presentation slide deck (~20-min talk) was designed for a visually-oriented sports science audience covering athlete monitoring and return-to-play data workflows. The design process resolved four key architectural decisions — framing, statistical thresholds, content constraints, and audience philosophy — and produced a locked 11-slide running order built around a single-athlete RTP narrative with minimal text and strong visual anchors. A subsequent validation pass confirmed all slides were layout-clean and fixed a dark-mode visibility bug on the final slide.

## Key Points

- **Single-athlete framing throughout:** roster-comparison views were explicitly rejected as "off-topic for the individual RTP framing." The presentation's decision-support narrative only holds together when the audience follows one athlete's trajectory from injury through return-to-competition decisions. Adding a roster view introduces a different clinical use case that fragments narrative coherence.
- **Visual-first audience philosophy:** the intended audience "eats with their eyes" — conversational delivery carries the explanatory load while slides provide visual anchors, not text. Minimal text per slide; strong imagery and color-coded indicators are the design primitives.
- **Z-score traffic-light thresholds: −1.5 SD / −2 SD.** Applied in the Excel demo to translate raw metrics into actionable status flags. −1.5 SD = caution/yellow; −2 SD = concern/red. The leave-behind template implements the same logic, ensuring the presentation and the artifact practitioners actually use share the same statistical foundation.
- **Screenshots-only (no live build):** consistent with the leave-behind template format. All data visualization examples appear as screenshots rather than live-built charts, eliminating technical failure risk in a conference setting.
- **11-slide running order:** bridge → decision-first framing (×2) → generalizing → metric selection → blank template → populated/flagged → charted → stakeholder report → take-home materials → close.
- **Slide 9 — Sample Stakeholder Report:** single-athlete trend chart + color-coded status flag + one plain-language interpretive line. Models the exact artifact the audience would produce and deliver to coaching/medical staff, completing the "here is the workflow" → "here is the output" arc.
- **Josse referenced verbally only (not on-screen):** a named methodological reference was kept off slides for sensitivity reasons; verbal attribution suffices for academic credentialing without creating a circulating visual artifact.
- **Slide validation (Session 23:56):** All 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667. Synthetic keyboard event dispatch (`keydown`) is unreliable for slide navigation in browser automation — smooth-scroll does not complete on synthetic key events in browser extension automation contexts. Use direct navigation-dot element clicks for reliable automated HTML slide deck validation.
- **Dark-background slides require adaptive nav chrome:** Slide 11 uses a dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`); the default nav-dot and slide-counter colors (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`) are invisible against it. Fix: an `on-dark` CSS class toggled on `<body>` by the `setActive()` JavaScript function enables CSS overrides for nav elements on dark slides. This pattern generalizes to any HTML slide deck with alternating light/dark slide backgrounds.

## Details

The presentation's core design challenge is bridging the gap between analytical rigor and practitioner legibility for a mixed audience of sports scientists, athletic trainers, and coaches. A talk that leads with methodology (sensor setup, reliability coefficients, statistical assumptions) loses practitioners in the first two minutes; a talk that shows only colored flags without any basis loses the sports scientists. The "decision-first framing (×2)" in the running order addresses this: the talk opens with the end product — the practitioner's decision — and only then traces backward to the analytical workflow that supports it. The repetition reinforces the framing before technical detail begins.

The z-score threshold design (−1.5 / −2 SD) was chosen for the Excel demo because it is transferable: any clinician working with any monitoring dataset can understand and apply standard deviation cutoffs without statistical training beyond "how far from the average." The traffic-light metaphor (green/yellow/red) maps intuitively to go/caution/stop decisions without requiring the audience to interpret numbers directly. The leave-behind template implements the same −1.5 / −2 SD thresholds automatically, so practitioners who use it after the session are working with the same statistical logic demonstrated in the talk — reducing drift toward arbitrary threshold modification post-session.

Slide 9's stakeholder report design was added specifically to address the "so what do I hand to the coach/AT?" question that sports scientists routinely face after building a monitoring pipeline. The three-element structure (trend chart + status flag + one interpretive sentence) is the minimum viable stakeholder report: more complex outputs tend to go unread or generate confusion when shared with coaching staff who do not routinely interpret data visualizations. The time budget for the talk was kept deliberately soft — enriching content depth was prioritized over strict adherence to 20 minutes, on the premise that a substantive overrun is less damaging than a rushed, thin presentation for an engaged sports science audience. The frontend-slides skill was loaded after all content decisions were locked to execute the build phase.

Following the content design session (20:28), a validation pass (Session 23:56) confirmed all 11 slides rendered correctly at both standard and mobile viewport sizes. The initial browser automation approach used synthetic keydown events to navigate between slides — this proved unreliable because the presentation's smooth-scroll transition does not complete when triggered by a synthetic key event in browser extension automation contexts. Switching to direct navigation-dot element clicks resolved this. A dark-mode visibility bug was discovered on Slide 11, whose dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`) made both the slide counter text and the inactive navigation dots invisible in their default dark-gray color (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`). The fix uses a `setActive()` JavaScript function that toggles an `on-dark` class on the `<body>` element each time a new slide becomes active, enabling CSS rules to override counter and dot colors when on a dark-background slide. This pattern — a JS class toggle driving CSS overrides for the nav chrome — is the correct approach for HTML slide decks that mix light and dark slide backgrounds: fixed CSS color values for UI elements will fail on at least one background type, while a theme-aware JS class toggle adapts correctly to each slide's context. The same failure class was independently encountered in the Swiss Modern coaching staff deck built the same day; see [[concepts/sports-coaching-slide-design-system]] for the `box-sizing` and `file://` URL gotchas encountered during that deck's construction.

- [[concepts/tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring]] — SPC-based monitoring dashboard with first-class explainability requirements for coaching and medical staff; shares the "every metric needs a plain-language justification" communication principle and threshold-based flag logic.
- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — The dual-model (actual vs. compliant counterfactual) ACWR overlay is another athlete monitoring communication artifact designed to make statistical content interpretable for practitioners — the same decision-support framing used in the presentation.
- [[connections/athlete-monitoring-communication-grammar]] — The cross-cutting visual vocabulary (color coding, threshold flags, trend + flag + sentence) that independently recurs across the presentation, Zinnecker reports, Tezino SPC monitoring, and the Swiss Modern coaching deck.
- [[concepts/sports-coaching-slide-design-system]] — A parallel S&C coaching staff slide deck built the same day (Session 23:43) using the Swiss Modern preset; shares the traffic-light color constraint and HTML slide build context. The two projects together document complementary implementation gotchas: coaching deck (box-sizing, file:// URL mangling) and RTP presentation (synthetic keydown unreliability, dark-background CSS toggle).

# Connection: A Contaminated Reference Window Silently Rewrites the Load Narrative

## The Connection

Two Baylor sports-science reporting builds — the Women's Tennis ACWR pipeline ([[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]]) and the Skylar Zinnecker CMJ return-to-competition reports ([[concepts/skylar-zinnecker-cmj-rtc-reports]]) — both turned on a single non-obvious point: the *window you compare against* is a design decision that changes the conclusion the report delivers, not a neutral technical detail. In the ACWR build, the compliant counterfactual ramp initially inherited real fall load because the overlay started inside the 7-day acute window, making the modeled compliant peak appear as 1.69 instead of the true 1.28 — a contaminated reference silently importing history into a hypothetical. In the Zinnecker build, moving the baseline from a 2-year historical average to the last 4 pre-injury sessions flipped Lower-Limb Stiffness from "Progressing (⚠)" to "Exceeds Baseline (✓)," because the new baseline (4,693) sat below the old one (5,477).

## Key Insight

The shared lesson is that a reference window is only trustworthy if it is *scoped to exactly the comparison you intend to make* — and that scoping error and honest scoping look identical in the final chart. The ACWR counterfactual is only valid once it contains no real training data; the fix was to anchor its first point at the date the last real load rolls off the acute window. The CMJ baseline is only clinically meaningful once it reflects the athlete's healthy pre-injury capacity rather than a smeared multi-year average that includes both peak and decline. In both cases the number that staff read off the report — "how compliant is this ramp?" / "has this metric recovered?" — is entirely a function of what got included in the reference, and a plausible-looking output can encode a contaminated one. The practical guard is the same in both domains: state explicitly what the baseline/reference *should* contain, then verify no out-of-scope data (real load, post-injury sessions, the wrong time range) leaked in before trusting the comparison.

## Key Points

- A reference window is a decision, not a default: both the ACWR chronic/counterfactual baseline and the CMJ pre-injury baseline changed the reported status of a metric without any change to the underlying athlete data.
- Contamination is invisible in the output: the 1.69 "compliant" peak and the "Progressing" stiffness status both looked plausible and were both artifacts of the wrong window.

# Claude Code Environment Maintenance

Periodic maintenance of the Claude Code environment surfaces configuration-drift issues that accumulate silently between active sessions. Four notable maintenance passes have been documented: a 2026-06-10 session that resolved plugin cache migration, stale MCP authentications, and temp-directory accumulation; a 2026-06-03 session that diagnosed and resolved a missing `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` for the GitHub MCP plugin; a 2026-06-09 session that switched the default model to Fable 5 and discovered that the advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with Fable 5 requests; and a 2026-07-09 observation of the GitHub MCP plugin failing to reconnect with an HTTP 401 because a configured `Authorization` header disables OAuth fallback. Most issues are caught via `/doctor` and resolved through `/mcp`, `/plugins`, or targeted configuration changes.

## Key Points

- `/doctor` flagged 4 issues on 2026-06-10: three claude.ai MCP servers (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar) needing re-authentication, and the `cli-printing-press` plugin not found at its expected versioned cache path.
- Claude Code migrated its plugin cache from a flat layout (`cache\<plugin>\`) to a versioned layout (`cache\<plugin>\<plugin>\<version>\`), likely due to a Claude Code update. Plugins installed under the old layout fail version checks even though their skills may still work via a fallback path; the fix is to reinstall via `/plugins`.
- Four stale `temp_github_*` directories were found in the plugins cache, left over from interrupted installs in late May/early June — safe to delete once confirmed unused. Interrupted plugin downloads can both lose a plugin's cache entry and leave orphan `temp_github_*` folders; `/plugin` reinstall + `/reload-plugins` restores the cache, and the orphan folders require manual deletion.
- For MCP servers not actively used from Claude Code (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar), disconnecting them in claude.ai's connector settings permanently silences `/doctor` re-auth warnings and eliminates the tool-schema token overhead of loading unused MCP tool definitions each session.
- The `compound-engineering` plugin was installed via `/plugin` and activated with `/reload-plugins`, adding `ce-*` skills/agents for planning, code review, commits, and PR workflows. `/effort` was set to "high" as the new session default.
- **GitHub MCP plugin vs. `gh` CLI (2026-06-03):** the `github@claude-plugins-official` MCP plugin requires a `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable to pass `/doctor`. If all GitHub operations use the `gh` CLI directly (authenticated via `gh auth login`; scopes: gist, read:org, repo, workflow), the MCP plugin is redundant — the cleanest fix is disabling it with `"github@claude-plugins-official": false` in `.claude/settings.json`. Alternatively, set `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` from an existing PAT (e.g., reuse `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` if it has matching scopes).
- **Fable 5 + medium effort + advisor incompatibility (2026-06-09):** default model switched to Fable 5, effort set to medium. The advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with the Fable 5 request model — requests return 400 errors — and was disabled. When switching request models, the advisor model must also be verified for compatibility or disabled; mismatched advisor+request combinations produce API errors that are not immediately obvious as a configuration conflict.
- **GitHub MCP 401 with Authorization header disables OAuth (2026-07-09):** the `plugin:github:github` MCP server failed to reconnect with HTTP 401 — the server rejected the configured `Authorization` header, and OAuth fallback is disabled whenever `headers.Authorization` is explicitly set. ## Details

The `/doctor` command acts as a quick health check across MCP connections, plugin installs, and cache state. On 2026-06-10 it caught a cache-format mismatch that was not the user's fault: a Claude Code update changed how plugins are cached on disk (from a flat directory per plugin to a versioned subdirectory), and `cli-printing-press` had been installed before that change. The plugin's files were technically present, but the version-check logic looked in the new versioned path and didn't find them — the recommended fix was simply to reinstall the plugin via `/plugins` so it lands in the new layout. The MCP re-auth findings (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar) were treated as low priority: rather than re-authenticating connectors that may not be exercised from Claude Code at all, the suggested path was to disconnect them at the source (claude.ai connector settings), which both stops the recurring `/doctor` warning and reduces the standing tool-schema footprint in every session.

Note: `setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately but requires fully restarting VS Code for the change to propagate to the Claude Code process — see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] for the stale-environment gotcha this can trigger.

# Connection: Windows Process Environment Is Fixed at Launch Time

## The Connection

On 2026-06-03, setting `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` via `setx` and then opening a new terminal tab inside VS Code failed to expose the updated value — because VS Code and its children inherited their environment snapshot at VS Code's launch time, not from the current registry state (see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]). On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hook setup required calling `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) because Claude Code's hook runner launches with a minimal bash environment that does not include the user's interactive-shell PATH customizations (see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]). On 2026-05-13, GSD generated hooks using PowerShell syntax because the tool observed the user's interactive shell at install time — but Claude Code's hook executor is a bash process that does not reflect the interactive shell's type or configuration (see [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]). On 2026-06-11, Windows Task Scheduler's morning cadence task failed silently when `pwsh.exe` was used as the executable — because Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal system environment that does not include user PATH entries, requiring the full absolute path `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe` (see [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]).

## Key Insight

All four incidents express the same underlying behavior of the Windows (and general POSIX) process model: **a process's environment is determined at spawn time and does not update when the system's configuration subsequently changes.** The failure manifests differently in each case — a `setx` value missing in VS Code's terminal, a binary absent from a hook's PATH, a hook command written for the wrong shell, an executable not found by a scheduled task — but the root cause is identical. The developer changes the system state (writes a registry key, installs a tool to PATH, configures an interactive shell, installs a runtime) and expects a running or freshly-spawned process to reflect that change. It doesn't, because each process type (long-running GUI app, hook runner, Task Scheduler action) has its own frozen environment snapshot, and these snapshots can differ from each other and from the "current" system state simultaneously.

The non-obvious implication for Claude Code tooling and Windows automation: every layer of the toolchain has its own frozen environment at spawn time. The `setx` issue means a running VS Code doesn't see new registry values; the hook-PATH issue means the hook runner doesn't see the interactive shell's PATH; the Task Scheduler issue means the scheduler doesn't see the user PATH at all, only the machine-level system PATH. All four require the same diagnostic question — "when was this process spawned, and what did the system look like then?" — rather than "what does the system look like now?" The preventive rule across all cases: never rely on the ambient environment of a spawned process; always use absolute paths, explicit environment setup, or fully-qualified invocations.

# Connection: Sports-Tech Vendor Integration Friction at Baylor

## The Connection

Baylor Athletics integrates with several major sports-technology vendors for athlete monitoring data: Catapult (GPS/load), Perch (weight room performance), Kitman (athletic training utilization), and — as of 2026-08-02 — Kinexon (volleyball player tracking). Each has surfaced a distinct integration friction pattern. Catapult's token model silently expires — documented in [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] and the broader [[connections/catapult-token-friction-across-baylor-projects]]. Perch's auth scheme worked backwards from all initial assumptions — documented in [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]]. Kitman offers no direct API access at all, requiring vendor mediation for every pull — documented in [[concepts/at-utilization-benchmarks-project]]. Kinexon exposes a REST API but keeps its docs, endpoints, and credentials non-public, released only through the customer success manager — documented in [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]].

## Key Insight

All four vendors share a common anti-pattern: naive integration assumptions fail, and the failure is not discoverable from documentation alone — it requires empirical discovery through an actual integration attempt or, in Kitman's and Kinexon's cases, a human/contractual channel. The failure modality differs by vendor, and the appropriate strategic response is calibrated to the friction type:

- **Kitman (vendor-mediation):** no API exists at this contract tier; design for a single comprehensive, precisely-specified request rather than iterative pulls. Every field omitted costs a full vendor-mediation round trip. The access constraint is also leverage for contract renegotiation.
- **Kinexon (gated docs):** a REST API exists but its documentation, endpoints, and bearer-token credentials are non-public and released only via the CSM. The correct interim strategy is to build against the documented CSV export (aided by open-source parsers like floodlight) while awaiting CSM-provided API access — decoupling schema/dashboard work from the credential wait.
- **Catapult (silent expiry):** tokens look valid but may be silently revoked; verify token freshness actively rather than assuming validity based on format or absence of an explicit expiry error. Integration tokens (shown once, non-refreshable) differ from OAuth tokens (60-minute lifecycle) in ways not obvious from the token's appearance.
- **Perch (backwards assumption):** a token that looks truncated or broken may be valid; the expected auth scheme (`JWT`) may not be the one that works (`Bearer`). Probe the live API with multiple auth schemes rather than inferring from token format.

The meta-pattern: sports-tech vendor APIs tend to be designed for their own client workflows, not for third-party integration. Documentation does not fully describe edge cases, token lifecycle constraints, access tier limitations, or is withheld entirely behind a human gatekeeper. Treating the first integration attempt as discovery rather than production — and budgeting calendar time for empirical verification of credentials and data shape, or for a vendor round trip — is the correct methodology for any new Baylor sports-tech vendor integration. # Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Athlete Monitoring / Return-to-Play Conference Presentation Design

On 2026-06-17, a conference presentation slide deck (~20-min talk) was designed for a visually-oriented sports science audience covering athlete monitoring and return-to-play data workflows. The design process resolved four key architectural decisions — framing, statistical thresholds, content constraints, and audience philosophy — and produced a locked 11-slide running order built around a single-athlete RTP narrative with minimal text and strong visual anchors. A subsequent validation pass confirmed all slides were layout-clean and fixed a dark-mode visibility bug on the final slide.

## Key Points

- **Single-athlete framing throughout:** roster-comparison views were explicitly rejected as "off-topic for the individual RTP framing." The presentation's decision-support narrative only holds together when the audience follows one athlete's trajectory from injury through return-to-competition decisions. Adding a roster view introduces a different clinical use case that fragments narrative coherence.
- **Visual-first audience philosophy:** the intended audience "eats with their eyes" — conversational delivery carries the explanatory load while slides provide visual anchors, not text. Minimal text per slide; strong imagery and color-coded indicators are the design primitives.
- **Z-score traffic-light thresholds: −1.5 SD / −2 SD.** Applied in the Excel demo to translate raw metrics into actionable status flags. −1.5 SD = caution/yellow; −2 SD = concern/red. The leave-behind template implements the same logic, ensuring the presentation and the artifact practitioners actually use share the same statistical foundation.
- **Screenshots-only (no live build):** consistent with the leave-behind template format. All data visualization examples appear as screenshots rather than live-built charts, eliminating technical failure risk in a conference setting.
- **11-slide running order:** bridge → decision-first framing (×2) → generalizing → metric selection → blank template → populated/flagged → charted → stakeholder report → take-home materials → close.
- **Slide 9 — Sample Stakeholder Report:** single-athlete trend chart + color-coded status flag + one plain-language interpretive line. Models the exact artifact the audience would produce and deliver to coaching/medical staff, completing the "here is the workflow" → "here is the output" arc.
- **Josse referenced verbally only (not on-screen):** a named methodological reference was kept off slides for sensitivity reasons; verbal attribution suffices for academic credentialing without creating a circulating visual artifact.
- **Slide validation (Session 23:56):** All 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667. Synthetic keyboard event dispatch (`keydown`) is unreliable for slide navigation in browser automation — smooth-scroll does not complete on synthetic key events in browser extension automation contexts. Use direct navigation-dot element clicks for reliable automated HTML slide deck validation.
- **Dark-background slides require adaptive nav chrome:** Slide 11 uses a dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`); the default nav-dot and slide-counter colors (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`) are invisible against it. Fix: an `on-dark` CSS class toggled on `<body>` by the `setActive()` JavaScript function enables CSS overrides for nav elements on dark slides. This pattern generalizes to any HTML slide deck with alternating light/dark slide backgrounds.

## Details

The presentation's core design challenge is bridging the gap between analytical rigor and practitioner legibility for a mixed audience of sports scientists, athletic trainers, and coaches. A talk that leads with methodology (sensor setup, reliability coefficients, statistical assumptions) loses practitioners in the first two minutes; a talk that shows only colored flags without any basis loses the sports scientists. The "decision-first framing (×2)" in the running order addresses this: the talk opens with the end product — the practitioner's decision — and only then traces backward to the analytical workflow that supports it. The repetition reinforces the framing before technical detail begins.

The z-score threshold design (−1.5 / −2 SD) was chosen for the Excel demo because it is transferable: any clinician working with any monitoring dataset can understand and apply standard deviation cutoffs without statistical training beyond "how far from the average." The traffic-light metaphor (green/yellow/red) maps intuitively to go/caution/stop decisions without requiring the audience to interpret numbers directly. The leave-behind template implements the same −1.5 / −2 SD thresholds automatically, so practitioners who use it after the session are working with the same statistical logic demonstrated in the talk — reducing drift toward arbitrary threshold modification post-session.

Slide 9's stakeholder report design was added specifically to address the "so what do I hand to the coach/AT?" question that sports scientists routinely face after building a monitoring pipeline. The three-element structure (trend chart + status flag + one interpretive sentence) is the minimum viable stakeholder report: more complex outputs tend to go unread or generate confusion when shared with coaching staff who do not routinely interpret data visualizations. The time budget for the talk was kept deliberately soft — enriching content depth was prioritized over strict adherence to 20 minutes, on the premise that a substantive overrun is less damaging than a rushed, thin presentation for an engaged sports science audience. The frontend-slides skill was loaded after all content decisions were locked to execute the build phase.

# Connection: A Contaminated Reference Window Silently Rewrites the Load Narrative

## The Connection

Two Baylor sports-science reporting builds — the Women's Tennis ACWR pipeline ([[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]]) and the Skylar Zinnecker CMJ return-to-competition reports ([[concepts/skylar-zinnecker-cmj-rtc-reports]]) — both turned on a single non-obvious point: the *window you compare against* is a design decision that changes the conclusion the report delivers, not a neutral technical detail. In the ACWR build, the compliant counterfactual ramp initially inherited real fall load because the overlay started inside the 7-day acute window, making the modeled compliant peak appear as 1.69 instead of the true 1.28 — a contaminated reference silently importing history into a hypothetical. In the Zinnecker build, moving the baseline from a 2-year historical average to the last 4 pre-injury sessions flipped Lower-Limb Stiffness from "Progressing (⚠)" to "Exceeds Baseline (✓)," because the new baseline (4,693) sat below the old one (5,477).

## Key Insight

The shared lesson is that a reference window is only trustworthy if it is *scoped to exactly the comparison you intend to make* — and that scoping error and honest scoping look identical in the final chart. The ACWR counterfactual is only valid once it contains no real training data; the fix was to anchor its first point at the date the last real load rolls off the acute window. The CMJ baseline is only clinically meaningful once it reflects the athlete's healthy pre-injury capacity rather than a smeared multi-year average that includes both peak and decline. In both cases the number that staff read off the report — "how compliant is this ramp?" / "has this metric recovered?" — is entirely a function of what got included in the reference, and a plausible-looking output can encode a contaminated one. The practical guard is the same in both domains: state explicitly what the baseline/reference *should* contain, then verify no out-of-scope data (real load, post-injury sessions, the wrong time range) leaked in before trusting the comparison.

## Key Points

- A reference window is a decision, not a default: both the ACWR chronic/counterfactual baseline and the CMJ pre-injury baseline changed the reported status of a metric without any change to the underlying athlete data.
- Contamination is invisible in the output: the 1.69 "compliant" peak and the "Progressing" stiffness status both looked plausible and were both artifacts of the wrong window.
- The fix is scope discipline: anchor the counterfactual only after real load clears the acute window; scope the CMJ baseline to the 4 pre-injury sessions clinically relevant to the RTC question.
- The stakes are narrative: these reports drive coaching/medical decisions, so a contaminated baseline can mislead staff about how achievable a compliant ramp is or whether an athlete has actually recovered.

## Details

The ACWR case is contamination by *temporal* leakage: the counterfactual is supposed to be a purely hypothetical trajectory, but because ACWR's acute window is a trailing 7 days, starting the overlay too early let real historical peaks bleed into the modeled path. The Zinnecker case is contamination by *composition*: a 2-year average is not wrong arithmetically, but it answers the wrong question for a return-to-competition assessment, where the relevant reference is the athlete's healthy pre-injury self, not a lifetime blend. Both are failures of matching the reference window to the intended comparison, and both were caught only by reasoning about what the window *ought* to contain rather than by inspecting the plotted line.

This generalizes beyond these two builds. Any monitoring output that reports "elevated / recovered / compliant / at-risk" is implicitly comparing current state to a baseline, and the baseline's construction is where the interpretive work — and the errors — live. The discipline that fixed both reports is to make the baseline's contents an explicit, defensible statement ("maintenance load through break, then rebuild"; "last 4 pre-injury sessions") and to audit for out-of-scope data before shipping, because the chart itself will never reveal the contamination.

# Claude Code Environment Maintenance

Periodic maintenance of the Claude Code environment surfaces configuration-drift issues that accumulate silently between active sessions. Four notable maintenance passes have been documented: a 2026-06-10 session that resolved plugin cache migration, stale MCP authentications, and temp-directory accumulation; a 2026-06-03 session that diagnosed and resolved a missing `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` for the GitHub MCP plugin; a 2026-06-09 session that switched the default model to Fable 5 and discovered that the advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with Fable 5 requests; and a 2026-07-09 observation of the GitHub MCP plugin failing to reconnect with an HTTP 401 because a configured `Authorization` header disables OAuth fallback. Most issues are caught via `/doctor` and resolved through `/mcp`, `/plugins`, or targeted configuration changes.

## Key Points

- `/doctor` flagged 4 issues on 2026-06-10: three claude.ai MCP servers (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar) needing re-authentication, and the `cli-printing-press` plugin not found at its expected versioned cache path.
- Claude Code migrated its plugin cache from a flat layout (`cache\<plugin>\`) to a versioned layout (`cache\<plugin>\<plugin>\<version>\`), likely due to a Claude Code update. Plugins installed under the old layout fail version checks even though their skills may still work via a fallback path; the fix is to reinstall via `/plugins`.
- Four stale `temp_github_*` directories were found in the plugins cache, left over from interrupted installs in late May/early June — safe to delete once confirmed unused. Interrupted plugin downloads can both lose a plugin's cache entry and leave orphan `temp_github_*` folders; `/plugin` reinstall + `/reload-plugins` restores the cache, and the orphan folders require manual deletion.
- For MCP servers not actively used from Claude Code (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar), disconnecting them in claude.ai's connector settings permanently silences `/doctor` re-auth warnings and eliminates the tool-schema token overhead of loading unused MCP tool definitions each session.
- The `compound-engineering` plugin was installed via `/plugin` and activated with `/reload-plugins`, adding `ce-*` skills/agents for planning, code review, commits, and PR workflows. `/effort` was set to "high" as the new session default.
- **GitHub MCP plugin vs. `gh` CLI (2026-06-03):** the `github@claude-plugins-official` MCP plugin requires a `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable to pass `/doctor`. If all GitHub operations use the `gh` CLI directly (authenticated via `gh auth login`; scopes: gist, read:org, repo, workflow), the MCP plugin is redundant — the cleanest fix is disabling it with `"github@claude-plugins-official": false` in `.claude/settings.json`. Alternatively, set `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` from an existing PAT (e.g., reuse `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` if it has matching scopes).
- **Fable 5 + medium effort + advisor incompatibility (2026-06-09):** default model switched to Fable 5, effort set to medium. The advisor model (opus-4-8) is incompatible with the Fable 5 request model — requests return 400 errors — and was disabled. When switching request models, the advisor model must also be verified for compatibility or disabled; mismatched advisor+request combinations produce API errors that are not immediately obvious as a configuration conflict.
- **GitHub MCP 401 with Authorization header disables OAuth (2026-07-09):** the `plugin:github:github` MCP server failed to reconnect with HTTP 401 — the server rejected the configured `Authorization` header, and OAuth fallback is disabled whenever `headers.Authorization` is explicitly set. Fix: check/refresh the token, or remove the `headers.Authorization` config entirely to re-enable OAuth negotiation.

## Details

The `/doctor` command acts as a quick health check across MCP connections, plugin installs, and cache state. On 2026-06-10 it caught a cache-format mismatch that was not the user's fault: a Claude Code update changed how plugins are cached on disk (from a flat directory per plugin to a versioned subdirectory), and `cli-printing-press` had been installed before that change. The plugin's files were technically present, but the version-check logic looked in the new versioned path and didn't find them — the recommended fix was simply to reinstall the plugin via `/plugins` so it lands in the new layout. The MCP re-auth findings (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar) were treated as low priority: rather than re-authenticating connectors that may not be exercised from Claude Code at all, the suggested path was to disconnect them at the source (claude.ai connector settings), which both stops the recurring `/doctor` warning and reduces the standing tool-schema footprint in every session.

On 2026-06-03, a separate `/doctor` run flagged the `github@claude-plugins-official` MCP server as invalid — specifically, no `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable was set. Investigation confirmed that all GitHub interactions in this environment already flow through the `gh` CLI (authenticated separately in `~/.config/gh/`), making the GitHub MCP plugin effectively unused. The two resolution options are: (1) disable the plugin entirely in `.claude/settings.json` — the simplest fix when the plugin genuinely adds no value; or (2) set `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` using an existing PAT with compatible scopes, avoiding a new token generation. In this case, `CODEX_GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` already existed with sufficient scopes, so `setx GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN <value>` was used. Note: `setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately but requires fully restarting VS Code for the change to propagate to the Claude Code process — see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] for the stale-environment gotcha this can trigger.

On 2026-06-09, a maintenance session switched the default model from Sonnet-tier to Fable 5 and changed effort to medium. The advisor feature, which provides secondary-model review of responses, uses a separately-specified model (opus-4-8 in this configuration). When the request model is Fable 5, the opus-4-8 advisor returns 400 API errors because the two models are incompatible in the advisor/request pairing. The advisor was disabled as a result. The lesson: model switches require verifying the full model configuration stack — not just the primary request model but also any secondary models (advisor, sub-agent defaults, tool-use overrides) that may have incompatible pairings.

On 2026-07-09, the GitHub MCP plugin surfaced a distinct failure mode from the 2026-06-03 missing-token case: here a token/header *was* configured, but the plugin failed to reconnect with HTTP 401 because the server rejected the supplied `Authorization` header. The non-obvious mechanism is that setting `headers.Authorization` explicitly disables the plugin's OAuth fallback — the plugin assumes a manually-supplied header means the user wants header-based auth exclusively, so it does not fall back to OAuth negotiation when the header is rejected. The result is a hard 401 with no automatic recovery. The two fixes are to refresh the token behind the header, or to remove the `headers.Authorization` config so OAuth negotiation is re-enabled. This reinforces the broader 2026-06-03 finding that the GitHub MCP plugin is often redundant when `gh` CLI already handles all GitHub operations — disabling the plugin outright sidesteps both the missing-token and the header-401 failure modes.

Together these maintenance passes confirm the same operational pattern: the `/doctor` command's value is proportional to how regularly it is run and how promptly its findings are triaged. Issues like the plugin cache migration, the unused GitHub MCP plugin, the advisor incompatibility, the header-401 reconnect failure, and the orphan temp folders can accumulate silently for weeks without causing visible failures, but each unresolved warning represents either a real reliability risk or unnecessary token overhead that degrades session quality.

# Connection: Windows Process Environment Is Fixed at Launch Time

## The Connection

On 2026-06-03, setting `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` via `setx` and then opening a new terminal tab inside VS Code failed to expose the updated value — because VS Code and its children inherited their environment snapshot at VS Code's launch time, not from the current registry state (see [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]). On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` hook setup required calling `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) because Claude Code's hook runner launches with a minimal bash environment that does not include the user's interactive-shell PATH customizations (see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]). On 2026-05-13, GSD generated hooks using PowerShell syntax because the tool observed the user's interactive shell at install time — but Claude Code's hook executor is a bash process that does not reflect the interactive shell's type or configuration (see [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]). On 2026-06-11, Windows Task Scheduler's morning cadence task failed silently when `pwsh.exe` was used as the executable — because Task Scheduler spawns processes with a minimal system environment that does not include user PATH entries, requiring the full absolute path `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe` (see [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]).

## Key Insight

All four incidents express the same underlying behavior of the Windows (and general POSIX) process model: **a process's environment is determined at spawn time and does not update when the system's configuration subsequently changes.** The failure manifests differently in each case — a `setx` value missing in VS Code's terminal, a binary absent from a hook's PATH, a hook command written for the wrong shell, an executable not found by a scheduled task — but the root cause is identical. The developer changes the system state (writes a registry key, installs a tool to PATH, configures an interactive shell, installs a runtime) and expects a running or freshly-spawned process to reflect that change. It doesn't, because each process type (long-running GUI app, hook runner, Task Scheduler action) has its own frozen environment snapshot, and these snapshots can differ from each other and from the "current" system state simultaneously.

The non-obvious implication for Claude Code tooling and Windows automation: every layer of the toolchain has its own frozen environment at spawn time. The `setx` issue means a running VS Code doesn't see new registry values; the hook-PATH issue means the hook runner doesn't see the interactive shell's PATH; the Task Scheduler issue means the scheduler doesn't see the user PATH at all, only the machine-level system PATH. All four require the same diagnostic question — "when was this process spawned, and what did the system look like then?" — rather than "what does the system look like now?" The preventive rule across all cases: never rely on the ambient environment of a spawned process; always use absolute paths, explicit environment setup, or fully-qualified invocations.

## Evidence

- 2026-06-03 (~15:00): "`setx` writes to the Windows registry immediately, but only newly-launched processes read it. New terminal tabs inside an already-running VS Code still inherit the stale env from when VS Code launched. Must fully quit and reopen VS Code for children to see the updated variable." — [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]
- 2026-04-14: "Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`." — [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]
